analysis.one_liner: Removes oil and gas companies from a domestic manufacturer tax break.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would deny oil and gas companies a federal tax deduction worth billions, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in January 2007 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2004, Congress gave American manufacturers a lower effective tax rate by replacing export tax breaks struck down as illegal by world trade rules. Oil and gas producers were included in that break even though they had never benefited from the old export provisions, and the bill's findings call the result a "reverse windfall profits tax" on their record profits [S3]. This bill would strike oil, natural gas, and their primary products from the deduction [S2] [S3]. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and died there [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, since the change would raise revenue by taxing oil and gas profits at a higher effective rate; the bill's findings argue ordinary consumers were effectively subsidizing oil company windfall profits through the tax code [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code to deny the 2004 domestic production deduction for income from the sale or disposition of oil, natural gas, or their primary products, raising the effective tax rate on those companies [S2] [S3].

The bill's own findings state that oil and gas producers were made eligible for the rate reduction despite suffering no loss from the repealed export tax benefits, and that this has lowered the tax rate on the windfall profits they were enjoying [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and natural gas producers and refiners, who would lose a deduction that lowers their effective tax rate; some of that cost could be passed to consumers through fuel prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: Oil and gas companies could pass part of the higher effective tax rate through to consumers in the price of gasoline, natural gas, and petroleum products, though the size of any pass-through would depend on market conditions [S3].

The deduction was written to encourage domestic production, so removing it for the energy sector could slightly reduce after-tax returns on domestic oil and gas investment; the bill applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2007 [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a genuine anomaly: a manufacturer's tax break extended to oil companies that had lost nothing when the old export tax provisions were repealed [S3]. The direct cost falls on oil and gas companies in the form of a higher effective tax rate, with a possible small pass-through to consumers. The main weakness is not design but reach: it does nothing beyond the deduction and died without ever being considered.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Representative Jim McDermott introduced the bill on January 12, 2007 and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S1] [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the full action history shows no further steps after the committee referral [S4] [S5].
Congress adjourned on January 3, 2009 with the bill still in committee, so it never received a hearing or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers kept the effective tax rate reduction the bill would have removed, since the provision never moved; taxpayers gained nothing. The finding that oil companies enjoyed the break without having lost the repealed export benefits stands unreversed [S3] [S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers kept the tax break

for.name: Rep. Jim McDermott
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 12, 2007 and supported ending the oil and gas industry's eligibility for the domestic production deduction.

against.name: Rep. Charlie Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the referral and never scheduled it for consideration; no markup, hearing action, or vote appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan split never showed up in the record [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Oil and natural gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would deny them the domestic production deduction created in 2004, raising their effective tax rate on income from oil and gas sales. The industry's interest in keeping the break ran against taxpayers, who would otherwise collect the additional revenue [S3].
